headline: 62 to 74 Feet: Sea Bass Steady on the Reef Line, Tuna Still Sitting Past the Ridge
subhead: The nearshore wrecks are producing keeper sea bass on the drift, but the tuna bite stays out past Barnegat Ridge until that warm edge decides to come in.
body_markdown:
Sixty-two feet on the inshore corner of Sea Girt Reef, current running maybe half a knot, and my sounder is stacked with sea bass marks sitting tight to the rubble on the up-current side. That's the number that told me where to make my first drop this week, and it's the number I keep coming back to — this time of August, the bass haven't pushed out to the deeper structure yet, they're still working the shallow reef edges where the bait's been holding.

Twenty years of writing depths and bottom composition in a soggy notebook teaches you that sea bass don't move much until the thermocline shoves them, and right now the thermocline hasn't shoved. Sea Girt Reef, Axel Carlson Reef, and Shrewsbury Rocks are all fishing the same way — decent numbers of keepers in the 13-15 inch class, a few pushing better, on Gulp Peach or white 5-inch swimming mullets threaded on a bucktail teaser above a standard sea bass rig, dropped straight down and worked with short lifts off bottom. Nothing that's going to fill a cooler in an hour, but a steady pick if you're willing to move the boat when the marks thin out. I fished Triple Wrecks Tuesday morning on the last of an outgoing tide and had a mixed bag — good sea bass activity early, then it went quiet as the current slacked off. That's been the pattern all week: strong for the first hour or two of a moving tide, then you're re-anchoring or hunting a new piece to keep the bite going.

I'll be straight with you — it's not a banner week out there. The sea bass fishing is honest work, not a sure thing. You need to be willing to run between pieces, check three or four spots on the reef network before you find the one holding fish that morning, and not get married to a single number in the book just because it produced last trip.

Further out, past Barnegat Ridge, the story is different and less settled. There's a warm-water edge that's been sitting out that way most of the month, and it's the kind of thing that can turn a slow day into a good one if you time it right. The tuna — yellowfin mostly, with bluefin mixed in on some of the deeper humps toward Klondike — have been working that break, but getting to them and finding the exact seam has been hit or miss depending on which day you go. I made the run out toward Klondike over the weekend chasing exactly that pattern and came up with one bluefin on the troll and a long quiet stretch after — the temperature edge had slid a little from where it had been sitting, and I was a mile or two off it most of the day. That's the game with these midrange grounds. You're not fishing a fixed spot, you're fishing where the water sets up that day, and sometimes you guess wrong.

Mahi have been scattered thin around any floating structure or temp break you find between the Ridge and Klondike — nothing consistent enough to call a pattern yet, just fish showing up under the occasional weed line or piece of debris when you happen to run across it. If you're making that run, keep a spinning rod rigged with a small chartreuse jig or a strip bait ready, because those mahi won't wait around while you dig through a tackle bag.

Water's still warm enough to hold that edge out past the Ridge, and the wind's been cooperative — light out of the southwest most days, which keeps the ride out manageable and doesn't tear up the surface enough to blow the temp break apart. If that holds through the week, I'd expect the tuna bite to firm up rather than fade, especially on the troll-to-chunk transition in the evening hours when the sun drops and the bait gets nervous. But I wouldn't bank a trip on it without checking the latest position of that edge before you leave the dock — it's moved on me twice already this month.

For the guy who just wants fish in the box without burning four hours of fuel, I'd stay inshore this week. Work the reef network — Sea Girt, Axel Carlson, Shrewsbury Rocks, Triple Wrecks — on the moving tide, keep the boat mobile, and treat the sea bass bite as a morning program rather than an all-day soak. For the guy chasing tuna, understand you're gambling on where that warm pool sits the day you go, and Barnegat Ridge is your jumping-off point to find out — not necessarily where the fish will be.

Looking ahead, if the wind stays out of the southwest and that offshore edge holds its ground, I expect the tuna pattern past the Ridge toward Klondike to keep improving into next week. The reef bite should hold too, though I'd expect the bass to start sliding toward the deeper pieces as the month wears on and the shallow water starts to lose its edge. I'll have my numbers ready either way.
